To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the majority of telecommuters are not frequent telecommuters, and 2) telecommuters are more likely to continue telecommuting if they are satisfied with their telework arrangements, if they perceive that their managers support them, and if they perceive that telework is a viable option for them in the future.

telecenter users can be grouped into three clusters based on their engagement in telecommuting and four clusters based on their frequency of telecommuting, that the engagement clusters are significantly related to the frequency clusters, that the engagement in telecommuters is related to the frequency of telecommuters, and that the frequency of telework is related to telecommuter characteristics.

(1) telecommuting is not a single behavior; (2) telecommuting engagement is not a single variable; (3) telecommuting frequency is not a single measure of engagement; (4) telecommuters can be classified into distinct groups according to their level of engagement and their frequency of telecommuting.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of telecommuters who are engaged and frequent telecommuters and those who are not.

the question of how telecommuters are distributed across the population of potential telecommuters, and how this distribution is affected by the characteristics of the telecommuters, telecenters, and the telecommuters' work.
understanding how telecommuters engage with telecenters, and how often they do so.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
telecommuting is a highly individualized activity.

the more telecenters are managed as an integrated system and the less they are managed as a collection of individual sites, the greater the likelihood that telecommuters will be engaged in and frequent telecommuting.
there is no single pattern of telecommuting, but rather multiple patterns of telecommuters, which are associated with different management-related issues and different outcomes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
telecommuting is a complex phenomenon, and that a more nuanced understanding of the phenomenon is needed.
telecommuters can be divided into three engagement groups, and that each of these groups has four different levels of telecommuting frequency, for a total of 12 telecommuting patterns.
there is no one pattern of telecommuting.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the engagement and frequency of telecommuting are not independent of each other and that the frequency of telecommuters should be considered as an important variable when studying telecommuting.
telecommuting patterns are highly variable, and the variability may be more important than the overall level of telecommuting.
telecommuting engagement is not necessarily correlated with frequency of telecommuting.
